text:
A language model never sees your text. It's cut into tokens, tokens become vectors, and attention lets every vector look at every other. Each step is a choice with a cost, and this round asks you to defend it. Nineteen questions: fourteen worked through, and five quickly at the end.

Question one. What is tokenization, and why is subword tokenization standard? It splits text into the units a model reads, and every choice of unit trades vocabulary against length. Whole words need a vast vocabulary and still miss new ones. Build one from this track's seven other pages, three thousand words, and read the NLP page with it: fifteen percent of its words were never seen, hallucination among them, and each becomes the same unknown token. Characters never miss, but they make the page five times as long as subword tokens do, and attention's cost grows with the square: twenty-five times. Subwords split the difference: frequent words stay whole, and rare ones break into known pieces. A production tokenizer with two hundred thousand pieces cuts hallucination in two, and averages one point four tokens a word on this page. The vocabulary has a price too: each piece is a row of the embedding table, so at a width of four thousand and ninety-six, that's over eight hundred million weights. What goes in those rows is the next question.
